opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core challenge is that we've gone from evaluating models built for one narrow task to evaluating systems that are, in a sense, general-purpose, and our evaluation methods haven't caught up.

In classical machine learning, and in the learning theory I come from, you had a well-defined problem. You fix a distribution, a loss function, and a task. You hold out a test set, and you can make fairly rigorous statements about how the model will perform on future data drawn from the same distribution. With large language models, almost every one of those assumptions breaks. There's no single task, and there's no single distribution. The space of prompts people will actually send is vast and keeps shifting. Users are also adaptive. They probe the model, and some of them are actively adversarial. So even the question "what is the test set?" doesn't have a clean answer.

A second problem is contamination. These models are trained on huge chunks of the internet, and many benchmarks end up in the training data in some form. A high score may reflect real capability, memorization, or something in between, and it's often hard to tell which. Benchmarks also saturate quickly, so the field keeps chasing new leaderboards. That isn't the same as building a scientific understanding of what these systems can do.

The third challenge, which I care about a lot given my work on responsible AI, is that many of the properties we most want to measure aren't accuracy-like at all. Fairness, privacy, toxicity, robustness, and truthfulness are much harder to pin down with generative models than with, say, a lending classifier. When I worked on algorithmic fairness, you could say "equalize false rejection rates across these groups," and that was a precise, auditable definition. When the output is open-ended text, what does it mean for a model to be fair? Fair with respect to which prompts, which groups, and which notion of harm? You end up needing much more careful, context-specific definitions, and often some human judgment in the loop. Human judgment, in turn, brings cost, noise, and disagreement.

Then there's a growing practice of using models to evaluate models, LLM-as-judge. It's pragmatic, and I understand why people do it, since it scales. But it carries a certain circularity, and the judge may share the same blind spots as the system it's grading.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say we need to move away from treating evaluation as a single number on a leaderboard and toward something more like auditing. That means defining specific properties carefully, being explicit about the distribution of use you care about, testing adversarially, and accepting that evaluation is ongoing rather than a one-time stamp of approval. That's less satisfying than a clean theorem, but I think it's where the field has to go.

r001.rationale: The response says prompts are vast and shifting, users adapt or act adversarially, and there is no clean test set; it also notes that open-ended text complicates evaluation.

r002.rationale: It discusses benchmark scores and leaderboard chasing, but does not identify proliferation of scores across models and evaluation metrics as a problem for interpreting results.

r003.rationale: It describes fairness as requiring context-specific definitions, but does not connect that multiplicity to the multiplicity of LLM evaluation metrics.

r004.rationale: It recommends defining properties carefully and auditing, but does not recommend choosing distinct metrics to avoid redundant measurement.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we're in a somewhat uncomfortable position, because these are the most capable systems we've ever built and also probably the hardest to evaluate rigorously, and those two things are related.

Let me break it into a few pieces. The first challenge is that the space of things these models can do is essentially open-ended. With a classifier, you have a well-defined task, a held-out test set, and you measure accuracy. With a language model, the "task" is anything someone might type into it. So the whole classical machinery of train/test splits and generalization bounds, which is really where I come from, doesn't map cleanly. You can construct benchmarks, and people do, but any finite benchmark is a vanishingly small sample of what the model will actually be asked to do.

The second challenge, which follows directly from that, is contamination. These models are trained on an enormous fraction of the public internet, and the benchmarks are on the internet too. So when a model scores well on some reasoning or coding benchmark, you genuinely don't know whether you're measuring capability or recall. People try to address this with held-out or freshly constructed test sets, but there's a kind of arms race there, and the half-life of a clean benchmark is short.

The third thing I'd point to is that many of the properties we care most about are not really accuracy-like properties at all. We care about whether the model is truthful, whether it's harmful, whether it's fair across different populations, whether it leaks private information from its training data. Those are things my colleagues and I have thought about a lot in the context of algorithmic fairness and privacy, and even in the much simpler supervised setting, defining them formally is contested. For something like differential privacy, you at least have a crisp mathematical definition. For something like "is this model being honest," we don't, and so evaluation becomes a mix of human judgment, red-teaming, and proxies that may or may not track what you care about.

And then the fourth challenge is more of a methodological one. Increasingly we evaluate language models with other language models, because human evaluation at scale is too expensive. That's pragmatically necessary but a little circular, and the biases of the judge model become baked into your measurements in ways that are hard to audit.

If I were to summarize, I'd say we've gotten very good at producing numbers about these models, and much less good at knowing what those numbers mean. The thing I'd like to see the field move toward is treating evaluation as a scientific problem in its own right, with the kind of statistical care about sampling, uncertainty, and adversarial robustness that we'd apply to any other measurement, rather than as a leaderboard exercise.

r001.rationale: It says LLM tasks can be anything users type and any finite benchmark covers only a tiny sample of real use cases.

r002.rationale: It says evaluation produces numbers whose meaning is unclear, but does not identify a proliferation of scores across models and metrics as the source of that difficulty.

r003.rationale: It notes that fairness definitions are contested, but does not compare that multiplicity to a multiplicity of LLM evaluation metrics.

r004.rationale: It recommends more scientifically careful evaluation, but does not recommend choosing distinct, nonredundant metrics.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the biggest challenges is that we’re asking these models to do such a broad range of things that it’s hard to say what a good evaluation even looks like. For a more traditional machine learning problem, you might have a fairly well-defined task, a test set, and a measure of error. With a language model, somebody can ask for a summary, somebody else can ask for code, and somebody else can ask for advice. Those require very different notions of quality.

And even within a task, there are multiple dimensions. An answer can be fluent and convincing but factually wrong. It can be accurate but fail to follow the instructions. So reducing all of that to a single benchmark score can obscure things that matter.

There’s also the question of whether your evaluation really measures generalization. If benchmark questions, or things very similar to them, are in the training data, then strong performance is harder to interpret. And once people start optimizing against a benchmark, you have to ask whether improvements on that benchmark translate into improvements in actual use.

So I’d want evaluations tied to particular uses, with careful attention to the kinds of failures that matter in those settings. Human judgment has a role, but it’s expensive and people disagree. Using models to evaluate other models is appealing, but then you have to validate the evaluator. There isn’t an easy way around the underlying measurement problem.

r001.rationale: It says LLMs are used for a broad range of tasks with different notions of quality, making it hard to define a good evaluation.

r002.rationale: It discusses how a single benchmark score can obscure important qualities, but does not identify a proliferation of scores across models and metrics as a difficulty.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between LLM evaluation metrics and definitions of fairness in machine learning.

r004.rationale: It notes that different tasks and answer qualities require different evaluations, but does not recommend choosing distinct metrics to avoid redundancy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the main challenges is that we’re trying to evaluate systems whose range of possible uses is extraordinarily broad. For a more traditional machine learning problem, you can often specify the task, agree on a metric, and evaluate performance on held-out data. With a large language model, even deciding what constitutes a good answer can be difficult. Are we measuring factual accuracy, usefulness, reasoning, or the ability to follow instructions? Those aren’t always the same thing.

There’s also the question of whether a benchmark is really measuring generalization. If the evaluation questions, or close variants of them, appeared in the training data, a high score may tell us less than we think. And once people start optimizing for a benchmark, it can become less informative about performance in the world.

From the perspective of my interests in fairness and privacy, averages are particularly inadequate. A model can perform very well overall and still fail systematically for particular groups, or disclose sensitive information under particular prompts. Those failures may be rare, but consequential.

So I think we need multiple forms of evaluation: carefully designed benchmarks, adversarial testing, and observation in the actual setting where the model will be used. And we should be cautious about treating any single score as a comprehensive measure of how capable or trustworthy a system is.

r001.rationale: It says LLMs have an extraordinarily broad range of uses, but does not explain that the range of inputs and outputs makes it difficult to cover natural use cases in evaluation.

r002.rationale: It discusses choosing among evaluation dimensions and cautions against relying on one score, but does not identify a proliferation of scores across models and metrics as a difficulty in interpreting evaluations.

r003.rationale: It mentions fairness concerns, but does not compare multiple LLM evaluation metrics with multiple reasonable definitions of fairness.

r004.rationale: It recommends several evaluation approaches, but does not say to select metrics that measure distinct things in order to avoid redundancy.
